artworks.title: Exploring Our Ecosystem: Climate Change, Whales, and Us
artworks.description: Learn how watersheds and ecological networks connect people, environment, and plants, explore how human activity and climate change impacts ecological balance, and consider our collective responsibilities to protect the earth.

artworks.placeNote: The museum doesn’t say which room; we put it with Whales Today, where the self-guide sends you to learn about whales and ecology.

artworks.title: Whales Today
artworks.description: Dedicated to the science and behavior of whales, the threats they face today, ocean preservation and marine mammal conservation: bioacoustics, tagging, the sand table and an augmented-reality whale.
artworks.galleryName: Whales Today (Jacobs Family Gallery): the whale skeletons overhead, the life-size blue whale heart, the sand table and the science of living whales
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s map and guides put it.

artworks.title: Kobo, the blue whale skeleton
artworks.description: A 66-foot juvenile male blue whale, struck by a tanker off Nova Scotia and carried into Narragansett Bay in 1998. Its skeleton is the centerpiece of the Jacobs Family Gallery, hanging over the Lobby (you also see it from the Whales Today ramp on the Main Level). Only some 500 blue whales live in the North Atlantic.
artworks.galleryName: Whales Today (Jacobs Family Gallery): the whale skeletons overhead, the life-size blue whale heart, the sand table and the science of living whales
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s map and guides put it.

artworks.title: Life-size blue whale heart
artworks.description: A full-size model of a blue whale’s heart, the largest heart of any animal. The museum’s guide asks: how many people could safely fit inside it? It arrived in 2018 as the first piece of the new Whales Today gallery.
artworks.galleryName: Whales Today (Jacobs Family Gallery): the whale skeletons overhead, the life-size blue whale heart, the sand table and the science of living whales
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s map and guides put it.

artworks.title: Quasimodo, the humpback whale skeleton
artworks.description: A 37-foot male humpback, about 3 years old, that died in 1932 and was towed ashore in Westport. He has hung in the museum since 1936, first next to the Lagoda, and in the Jacobs Family Gallery since 2000.
artworks.galleryName: Whales Today (Jacobs Family Gallery): the whale skeletons overhead, the life-size blue whale heart, the sand table and the science of living whales
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s map and guides put it.

artworks.title: Reyna, the North Atlantic right whale, and her unborn calf
artworks.description: A 49-foot, 15-year-old female right whale, ten months pregnant with her first calf when a ship struck her in Chesapeake Bay. Her skeleton was hoisted to the Jacobs Family Gallery ceiling in 2008, with her calf’s beside her. Right whales are among the most endangered whales in the world.
artworks.galleryName: Whales Today (Jacobs Family Gallery): the whale skeletons overhead, the life-size blue whale heart, the sand table and the science of living whales
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s map and guides put it.

artworks.title: Boundless: The Book as Art

artworks.title: The City that Lit the World
artworks.description: This gallery charts the growth of New Bedford from a small coastal village to a booming city.
